opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a lot of it comes from how these claims get made in the first place. When a company announces that their model "understands" language or "reasons" like a human, what they usually have is a set of benchmark numbers, and those benchmarks are often pretty narrow. They measure performance on a specific dataset, under specific conditions, and then the headlines generalize that into something much bigger than what was actually tested.

There's also a real lack of transparency. Many of the most hyped models are closed, so we don't know what data they were trained on. That matters a lot, because if the test questions, or things very close to them, were in the training data, then a high score tells you more about memorization than capability. Without access to the data, independent researchers can't check that, and we're essentially asked to take the results on faith.

And then there are the incentives. There's an enormous amount of money and attention tied to being seen as the leader, so there's pressure to frame every incremental improvement as a breakthrough. Anthropomorphic language makes that worse. Words like "thinking," "knowing," or "being creative" set expectations the systems don't really meet, and people end up trusting them in situations where they shouldn't, like medical or legal advice.

My skepticism isn't about saying these models are useless. They can be really impressive and useful tools. I just think we need more rigorous, independent evaluation, more openness about data and costs, including environmental costs, and more honest language about what these systems actually do. Otherwise the conversation gets driven by marketing instead of science.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think a lot of it comes from how I came into the field. I started out doing research, I did my PhD, and then I spent a few years in industry before coming back to work on things like climate and the environmental impacts of AI. And what I noticed, especially in the last few years, is that the way we talk about progress has gotten really detached from how we actually measure it.

So you'll see a paper or a blog post or a press release that says a model has "human-level" performance on some task, or that it "understands" language, or that it can "reason." And when you actually dig into what's behind that claim, it's usually a number on a benchmark. And benchmarks are really useful tools, I'm not against them, but they're proxies. They were designed by people, at a specific moment, to capture some narrow slice of a capability. They have biases baked in, they have errors in the labels, and increasingly they're contaminated, because the test data has leaked into the training data at web scale and nobody can really verify that it hasn't.

So when someone says a model got 90 percent on a benchmark, that doesn't tell me very much about what it can do in the world. It tells me it did well on that particular set of questions, in that particular format. And then the marketing layer on top takes that number and turns it into "this model understands the world," which is a huge leap.

The other thing that makes me skeptical is the lack of transparency. A lot of the most hyped models right now, we don't know what they were trained on, we don't know how big they are, we can't reproduce the evaluations. And in any other scientific field, if you came in and said "trust me, it works, but I can't show you the data or the method," people would be pretty uncomfortable with that. But in AI we've sort of normalized it.

And then finally, I think it matters because these claims have consequences. They shape where funding goes, they shape policy, they shape what gets deployed in hospitals or in hiring. And they also justify the resources we're pouring into these systems, the compute and the energy and the water. If we're going to be using that much, I think we should at least be honest and rigorous about what we're actually getting for it. So my skepticism isn't about saying nothing is happening. There's real progress. It's about asking people to show their work.

astra-6.text:
I think we often make a leap from “this model performs well on a benchmark” to “this model understands language” or “this model can reason.” Those are very different claims. A benchmark tells you how a model performed on a particular set of examples, under particular conditions. It doesn’t necessarily tell you how it will behave when the context changes or when someone uses it for something the designers didn’t anticipate.

So I want to know what’s behind the claim. What was the model trained on? How was it evaluated? Could those evaluation examples have appeared in its training data? And what are the cases where it fails? If all we see is a polished demo or a single score, it’s hard to assess how meaningful an advance actually is.

That doesn’t mean the progress isn’t exciting. It means we should be precise about what we’ve demonstrated and what we’re inferring from it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we often conflate doing well on a benchmark with having a general capability. If a model passes an exam, for example, that’s an interesting result, but what does it actually tell us? Has it encountered those questions during training? Does it still do well if you change how they’re phrased? And does that performance translate to a real situation where there isn’t one clearly defined right answer?

My skepticism is really about the gap between what we can demonstrate and what we claim. These models can do impressive things, but we need to understand the conditions under which they work and where they fail. When we don’t have access to the training data or enough information to reproduce an evaluation, it’s difficult to assess those claims independently. I’d like to see more of that evidence before we make sweeping statements about intelligence or progress.
